To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) interactive game play activates mesolimbically-projecting regions of the caudate and nucleus accumben; 2) activation of the parahipppocampal subregion of the hippocampus correlates with positive attitudes toward cancer chemotherapy; and 3) the magnitude of mesolimbic reward circuit activation during interactive game play is significantly greater than during passive exposure to game-related sensory stimulation.

playing a videogame for cancer treatment patients (Re-Mission) robustly activates reward-related neural circuits associated with motivation and incentive processing, and that these effects stem primarily from the participatory nature of gameplay, rather than from the sensory/perceptual stimulation generated by the game’s dynamic event-stream.
playing a serious videogame activates reward-related mesolimibic neural circuits and that the magnitude of activation in these regions is correlated with positive attitudes toward cancer treatment.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of the interactivity and reward-related neural activation during a serious videogame.
the neural mechanisms of learning, and in particular, how learning is affected when a subject is actively engaged in the learning experience.
the neurobiological underpinnings of the effects of interactive digital games on the brain, and with the implications of these effects for serious games in health care and education.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this study demonstrates that interactivity is the key to the reward-related neural activation that occurs during serious videogame play.

this study found that playing an IDG activates reward-related brain areas, and that these activations are more pronounced in the interactive condition compared to a control condition where the same visual and auditory stimuli were passively presented.

the interactivity of a game, not the visual and audio components, is the key to activating the reward system of the brain, and that this reward system activation is related to positive attitudes toward cancer treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interactivity of the game is what drives the activation of the brain regions that we were interested in.

the mesolimbic reward circuitry is more activated during the active playgroup compared to the passive exposure control condition, suggesting that interactivity plays a role in the activation of this neural network.
the interactivity of the game was the most important factor in the activation of reward circuits.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interactivity of IDGs is a key factor in the activation of mesolimbic reward-related brain circuitry, which in turn appears to be associated with positive attitudes toward treatment.
interactivity in serious videogames may be a powerful tool for engaging reward-related brain regions in a manner that is likely to promote learning, retention and transfer of health information.
the participatory nature of IDGs can be leveraged to enhance their potential for therapeutic benefit.
